videos.title: Warsh Touts ‘Consequential’ AI, Trump Press Secretary Out After Five Days
videos.description:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh described AI as potentially the most consequential change to the US and global economy in his lifetime, calling it a positive supply shock over the medium term. We get reaction from Bloomberg's Enda Curran. One flagship AI data center in Norway is six months behind schedule, with workers set to be housed in a floating hotel to get it over the finish line. Bloomberg's Brody Ford explains. Katie Zacharia will no longer serve as President Donald Trump’s press secretary after spending less than a week on the job. Bloomberg's Skylar Woodhouse reports from the White House. Veda Partners' Henrietta Treyz examines the road to US midterms. Plus - Bloomberg News US Sports Reporter Randall Williams discusses the NFL's Fall Meeting and the mystery swirling around the next Super Bowl halftime headliner. All on the latest episode of Bloomberg Businessweek Daily.

videos.title: Ajay Banga's Plenary Remarks | 2026 Annual Meetings
videos.description:
In his Annual Meetings Plenary speech, World Bank Group President, Ajay Banga, outlined a development model centered on creating jobs at scale by bringing together public finance, private investment, philanthropy, and technology around country priorities. He highlighted progress in mobilizing private capital, expanding access to energy, health, and water, supporting MSMEs, and putting practical AI to work. His message: with 1.2 billion young people entering the workforce, development must move faster and deliver opportunity at scale.

ABOUT THE WORLD BANK 🌐 The World Bank is one of the world’s largest sources of funding and knowledge for low-income countries. Its five institutions share a commitment to reducing poverty, increasing shared prosperity, and promoting sustainable development on a livable planet. http://www.worldbank.org

videos.title: Why More Americans Regret College And Homeownership
videos.description:
For generations, mortgages and student loans have been held up as textbook examples of “good debt,".This borrowing promises to  build wealth or increase your earning power over time. On the other side of the coin is so-called “bad debt”, things like auto loans or credit card debt that don’t provide a financial return over time. As the costs of buying a home and getting a degree have continued to climb, more Americans are questioning whether those “good debt” investments are actually paying off.

Producer: Juhohn Lee
Reporter: Stephanie Dhue
Camera by: Macklin Fishman
Edited by: Nic Henry. Dennis Donovan
Animation: Jason Reginato, Emily Park
Senior Director of Video: Jessica Leibowitz

videos.title: Why This Tiny Robot Could Fix Massive Sewer Failures | WSJ
videos.description:
In January, a collapsed sewer pipe outside Washington, D.C., spilled more than 240 million gallons of raw sewage into the Potomac River. It is likely the largest sewage spill in U.S. history, but just one of an estimated 75,000 across the country each year, according to the EPA.

As aging sewer networks struggle with growing populations and changing weather patterns, a team of engineers and professors in Europe is developing a robot designed to detect and potentially address problems before disaster strikes.

WSJ explains how the $9 million EU-funded PIPEON project is tackling the dark and perilous world beneath our streets.

2:04 The Potomac River disaster and impact
3:31 Mapping the networks
4:47 The tech and details of the robot
6:16 What's next?

videos.title: Why There’s An ‘Extremely Fierce’ Battle For TSMC's Limited Chip Manufacturing Capacity
videos.description:
Unstoppable demand for AI is leading to a capacity crunch on factory lines at the world's leading chip manufacturer, Taiwan Semiconductor. And it could put a chokehold on AI's ability to scale. Analysts tell CNBC that Nvidia, Apple, Broadcom, AMD and others are locked in an “extremely fierce” competition to get their GPUs, CPUs and custom AI chips made at TSMC. Capacity can’t come online fast enough, despite TSMC’s rush to build new fabs in Taiwan, Japan and Arizona, where has expanded investment to $265 billion. The strain has made one man at TSMC “the most popular person on the planet,” as chip start-ups and big name CEOs visit Taiwan to ask him for wafer allocation. It’s also created a rich opportunity for Intel, as customers look to the long-struggling foundry arm of the U.S. chip manufacturer for a second source.

2:06 ‘Most popular person on the planet’
6:54 Making room for smaller players

videos.description:
